newsitem.title: USA: Clinton jokingly offers to jump off cliff for Weld.
newsitem.headline: Clinton jokingly offers to jump off cliff for Weld.

text.p: President Bill Clinton said on Wednesday former Massachusetts Gov. William Weld deserved a hearing to be considered as ambassador to Mexico and jokingly offered to jump off a cliff if that would help his candidacy.

But his endorsement of Weld, a moderate Republican, came in terms so mild it seemed unlikely to sway Sen. Jesse Helms, the conservative Republican chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee who has refused to schedule a hearing on the matter.
Asked at a news conference what he would do to help Weld's nomination, Clinton joked: "I thought maybe I'd go down to Mexico and jump off those cliffs at Acapulco."

Then, saying he wanted to make a serious comment on the matter, Clinton said Weld was a worthy candidate but stopped short of offering any carrots, or threatening any sticks, that might be used to change Helms' mind.

"I believe that Gov. Weld would be a good ambassador to Mexico and is rather uniquely situated to be a good ambassador to Mexico because of his background, his experience, his knowledge," Clinton said. "I think at least the man ought to get a hearing; he ought to get his day in court."

"We've got a team organised in the White House to try to help promote his nomination and we'll do the very best we can and we'll see what happens," he added. "I believe he ought to be the ambassador and I'm going to try to see him confirmed."
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright echoed Clinton's remarks.

"We -- President Clinton and I -- have believed, do believe that Gov. Weld is the best person for the job," she said on Wednesday. "We think it's very important that he have hearings and that the entire Senate be able to decide."
Clinton also said his overall relationship with Helms had been "good, and surprisingly constructive," suggesting that he would not publicly attack the Republican on Weld's behalf.
As chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee, Helms can refuse to schedule a committee hearing on Weld's nomination and prevent the matter from going to the full Senate.

Helms has argued that Weld is soft on drugs because of his support for medicinal uses of marijuana and therefore a poor choice for U.S. ambassador to Mexico, a major transit point for narcotics flowing into the United States.
Weld, however, has argued Helms' opposition is political. "This is about ideological purity and whether there is only one kind of Republican welcome in the Republican party," he said recently.
